vocab.title: Match each word to its meaning
defs: a small round stone used to build old streets
full of people, noise and energy
so special that you remember it for the rest of your life
an open public space in a city, with buildings all around
from the Middle Ages, between about the year 500 and 1500
extremely beautiful, in a way that surprises you
a protected place by the sea where boats stay
so beautiful that you stop and stare for a moment

paras: Ten years ago my wife and I spent three days in Split, on the coast of Croatia. We arrived late at night, and the taxi left us in front of a small door in a wall. Behind that door we found a whole city. The Romans built a palace there seventeen hundred years ago, and people still live inside it today.

In the morning the light was stunning. We walked on cobblestone streets between medieval houses, and every corner opened into a small square. At eleven we sat down in a cafe near the harbor and watched the fishing boats come back. An old man at the next table told us where to eat, and we took his advice.

That evening the town became lively. Families walked along the water, children ran between the tables, and four men sang old songs with no microphone at all. We ate grilled fish, we drank the local wine, and we didn't look at a map once. It was breathtaking, and it was unforgettable. Ten years later, I still remember the smell of that harbor.

bank.label: Useful sentences to tell a travel story
items: We arrived late at night and we walked straight into the old town.
It was absolutely stunning at that time of day.
What struck me most was the light on the old stone.
I couldn't believe how quiet the square was in the morning.
A few years ago I went there for the first time.
On my last trip, I ate at a small place near the harbor.
We didn't plan anything, and that was the best part.
I met a couple from Zagreb and we talked for an hour.

listenings.text: Last September I finally visited the town my grandmother talked about all her life. I took an early bus and arrived before the shops opened. The streets were empty, and the light on the old stone was stunning. I walked for two hours without a map. At noon I found a small square behind the cathedral, and I sat there with a coffee and a piece of cake. An old woman asked me where I was from, and we talked for twenty minutes. I understood almost everything she said. I did not want to leave. It was a short trip, but it was unforgettable.

Good morning, everyone. Before we walk down to the water, let me tell you how this harbor began. Fishermen built the first houses here more than eight hundred years ago. In the fifteenth century the town grew rich, and the families paid for the church you see on your right. Then, in sixteen sixty-seven, a strong earthquake destroyed almost everything. The people did not leave. They rebuilt the same streets, with the same stone, and they finished the work in less than thirty years. That is why the old town still looks medieval today.
